content: The Scent Girls program, targeting girls aged 9 to 13 years, provides an opportunity to verify if they have received the Measles-Rubella-Containing Vaccine (MRCV) and to administer it if they have not. When immunization efforts focus solely on adolescent girls or women of reproductive age (WRA), the overall epidemiology and circulation of the rubella virus remain largely unchanged. This approach leads to a linear decline in the incidence of congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) as vaccine coverage increases. However, achieving CRS elimination with this strategy alone is unlikely, as it would require immunizing every susceptible woman effectively. Healthcare workers, who frequently interact with pregnant women and may assist in delivering babies or caring for infants with CRS or congenital rubella infection (CRI), must be vaccinated. This is crucial to prevent them from transmitting rubella to unprotected pregnant women. Transmission in these outbreaks has occurred between healthcare workers, patients, and co-workers. Strategies to vaccinate healthcare workers include mandatory vaccination for employment, free or subsidized vaccines, serological testing with vaccination for those lacking immunity, and education on the benefits of vaccination. CRS surveillance should be established before or soon after MRCV introduction, though it is not a prerequisite for vaccine rollout. Detailed guidance on setting up CRS surveillance and investigating rubella outbreaks is available in relevant annexes. Before introducing rubella-containing vaccines (RCV) into national immunization programs, it is essential to review the epidemiology of rubella, assess the CRS burden, and plan for high vaccine coverage (≥95%). Healthcare workers must have clear policy guidance on rubella and measles strategies. Rubella vaccination should not be limited to infants under 12 months, as older children who missed earlier vaccinations must complete their schedules. Vaccination records should be maintained for all doses administered. School entry screenings should identify unvaccinated children, who should then be referred for missing vaccinations. WRA should also be screened and offered rubella vaccination during health system interactions, such as premarital screenings, postpartum visits, or when bringing infants for immunization. Rubella vaccination should be integrated into the routine immunization schedule as part of the MRCV, administered alongside the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1). Unvaccinated older children should receive MRCV whenever they access health services. Countries implementing a two-dose measles schedule are advised to use the combined MRCV for both doses to simplify logistics and improve coverage. The introduction of RCV requires updating national immunization plans, integrating rubella strategies with measles elimination efforts, and ensuring high coverage through routine immunization and supplementary immunization activities (SIAs). Comprehensive plans should address vaccination strategies, surveillance, cold chain capacity, communication, monitoring, and financing. Collaboration with education ministries and other stakeholders is essential for school-based vaccination programs. Rubella vaccine presentations include measles-rubella (MR), measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), and monovalent rubella vaccines, though the latter is not available through UNICEF. MR vaccines are supplied in 10-dose vials and require reconstitution with specific diluents. Vaccine supply forecasting should account for the same number of doses as measles vaccines, with adjustments for two-dose schedules or additional target groups like WRA and healthcare workers. Vaccine wastage rates, often high for multi-dose vials, should be monitored and minimized through strategies like vaccinating mothers during infant immunization visits. Cold chain capacity must be assessed and expanded if necessary to accommodate the additional vaccine volumes and injection supplies. Effective vaccine management plans should be developed at least a year before introducing new vaccines or campaigns. The introduction of MRCV as a replacement for measles-only vaccines simplifies logistics, as the packed volume remains similar. However, efforts to vaccinate WRA and healthcare workers may impact cold chain requirements. Countries should conduct wide-age-range MRCV campaigns before integrating the vaccine into routine immunization schedules. Vaccine wastage rates for campaigns are typically lower than routine immunization, and strategies to reduce wastage should be implemented. In summary, introducing rubella vaccines into national immunization programs requires comprehensive planning, integration with existing measles strategies, and efforts to achieve high coverage. This includes vaccinating healthcare workers, WRA, and missed populations, ensuring robust cold chain systems, and maintaining accurate vaccination records.
